essays.stem: Describe the main sectors of the tourism and hospitality industry in Jamaica, and give an example of a business in each.
essays.modelAnswer: The tourism and hospitality industry is made up of several sectors that work together to serve visitors. The accommodation sector provides places to stay, such as all-inclusive resorts, hotels, villas, guest houses and apartments. The food and beverage sector includes restaurants, jerk centres, bars and cafés, as well as the kitchens in hotels and villas. The transport sector moves visitors around: airlines, cruise lines, licensed tour buses, taxis and car rental firms. Attractions and entertainment include places such as Dunn's River Falls, river rafting, great houses, museums, music events and festivals. Tour operators and travel agents put together and sell trips and holiday packages. Other businesses, such as craft markets, spas and tour guides, also depend on visitors. All these sectors are linked: if one gives poor service, the visitor's whole holiday suffers.
markingPoints: Accommodation, with a correct example
Food and beverage, with a correct example
Transport, with a correct example
Attractions and entertainment, with a correct example
Tour operators and travel agents (or other visitor businesses), and how the sectors are linked

essays.stem: Compare three kinds of accommodation found in Jamaica, such as an all-inclusive resort, a villa and a guest house.
essays.modelAnswer: An all-inclusive resort is usually a large property with many rooms, pools, restaurants and bars. Guests pay one price that covers the room, meals, drinks and many activities, so they know the cost in advance, but they may not leave the resort much. A villa is a private house rented by one family or group. It often has its own staff, such as a cook, a housekeeper and a butler, and gives guests privacy, space and a personal service. Meals are often cooked to the guests' wishes, and guests can plan their own days. A guest house is a smaller, often family-run property with a few rooms. It is usually cheaper, gives a homely welcome, and may offer breakfast only, so guests eat out and meet local people. All three must meet the standards set for tourism businesses, and the staff in each must give friendly, safe service.
markingPoints: All-inclusive resort: large, one price for room, meals, drinks and activities
Villa: private house for one group, own staff, privacy and personal service
Guest house: small, often family-run, cheaper, homely, may offer breakfast only
Makes a clear comparison (price, size, privacy, meals or service)
Notes that all must meet tourism standards and give safe, friendly service

essays.stem: Describe three of Jamaica's main resort areas and what each offers visitors.
essays.modelAnswer: Montego Bay, in St James, is home to Sangster International Airport, so many visitors arrive there. It has many hotels and all-inclusive resorts, beaches, a cruise port, shopping, golf, and great houses such as Rose Hall. Ocho Rios, in St Ann on the north coast, is a busy cruise port and resort town. Visitors go to Dunn's River Falls, take river and nature tours, and visit gardens and beaches. Negril, at the western end of the island in Westmoreland and Hanover, is famous for Seven Mile Beach, its cliffs and its sunsets. It has a relaxed feel, with many small hotels, villas and water sports. Other areas include Port Antonio in Portland, known for rafting on the Rio Grande and the Blue Lagoon, and the south coast, with Treasure Beach and Black River. Kingston, the capital, offers music, history and culture.
markingPoints: Names three real resort areas with their correct parish or location
Montego Bay (or another area): correct main features
Ocho Rios (or another area): correct main features
Negril (or another area): correct main features
Says clearly what each area offers visitors (beaches, attractions, culture, cruise port)

essays.stem: Explain the roles of the Jamaica Tourist Board (JTB) and TPDCo in Jamaica's tourism industry.
essays.modelAnswer: The Jamaica Tourist Board (JTB) is the government agency that markets and promotes Jamaica as a place to visit. It runs advertising, takes part in travel fairs, works with airlines, cruise lines and travel agents, and has offices in the main markets abroad, such as North America and Europe. Its aim is to bring more visitors to Jamaica. The Tourism Product Development Company (TPDCo) looks after the tourism product: everything the visitor sees and experiences on the island. It works to improve attractions and resort areas, sets and checks standards for tourism businesses, and helps with licensing and inspections. TPDCo also trains people who work with visitors, through programmes such as Team Jamaica. Both bodies work with the Ministry of Tourism. In short, the JTB brings the visitors, and TPDCo helps make sure they have a safe, good-quality experience when they arrive, so that they come back and tell others.
markingPoints: JTB markets and promotes Jamaica as a destination
JTB methods: advertising, travel fairs, work with airlines and travel agents, overseas offices
TPDCo develops and improves the tourism product and resort areas
TPDCo sets and checks standards, helps with licensing, and trains workers (Team Jamaica)
Both work with the Ministry of Tourism; JTB brings visitors, TPDCo protects the quality of their stay

essays.stem: Explain how tourism benefits Jamaica and its communities, and give two problems it can cause.
essays.modelAnswer: Tourism is one of Jamaica's most important industries. It brings in money from abroad, which helps the country pay for the goods it imports. It creates many direct jobs in hotels, villas, restaurants, attractions and transport, and indirect jobs for farmers, fishermen, craft makers, builders and suppliers. Money spent by visitors helps small businesses in communities, and taxes from tourism help pay for roads, schools and health care. Tourism also encourages the protection of Jamaican culture, music, food and heritage, and gives workers the chance to learn new skills. However, tourism can cause problems. If it is not managed well, it can damage the environment through waste, pollution and harm to reefs and beaches. Some of the money may leave the country, for example when profits are sent abroad or food is imported. Other problems can include crowding, rising prices, and the harassment of visitors, which harms Jamaica's good name.
markingPoints: Earns money from abroad (foreign exchange)
Creates direct and indirect jobs, with links to farming, fishing and craft
Helps communities, small businesses, public services and culture
Problem 1: harm to the environment (waste, pollution, reefs, beaches)
Problem 2: money leaving the country, crowding, rising prices or visitor harassment

essays.stem: Describe the sources a villa worker can use to keep their industry knowledge up to date, and say why each is useful.
essays.modelAnswer: A villa worker can read news and updates from the Jamaica Tourist Board, TPDCo and the Ministry of Tourism, which give reliable information about new attractions, events and standards. Industry associations such as the JHTA share news about the trade. The tourism pages of newspapers and trusted news websites report on new hotels, airline routes and changes that affect tourism. Training courses, such as those from HEART/NSTA Trust and TPDCo's Team Jamaica, build new skills and give a recognised certificate. Supervisors and experienced colleagues share practical knowledge about the villa's own standards. Guest feedback and reviews show what visitors value and what can be improved. Visiting local attractions, restaurants and events lets the worker give honest, first-hand advice to guests. The worker should always check that a source is reliable and up to date, and not trust rumours on social media.
markingPoints: Official bodies (JTB, TPDCo, Ministry of Tourism) for reliable news and standards
Industry associations and newspapers for trade news
Training courses (HEART/NSTA Trust, Team Jamaica) for skills and certificates
Supervisors, colleagues and guest feedback for practical knowledge
First-hand visits, and checking that every source is reliable and current

essays.stem: Describe the main jobs in a staffed villa and how they work together.
essays.modelAnswer: A staffed villa may have a villa manager, a butler, a cook, one or more housekeepers, a gardener or pool attendant, a driver and security staff. The villa manager plans the work, deals with bookings and the owner, and makes sure standards are met. The butler looks after the guests' personal needs: greeting them, unpacking, serving drinks and meals, and passing on requests. The cook plans menus with the guests, buys food and prepares meals safely. The housekeeper cleans the rooms, makes the beds, does the laundry and reports any damage. The gardener keeps the grounds and the pool clean and safe. The driver takes guests on trips and to the airport, and security staff protect the guests and the property. They work together by sharing information at a daily briefing and in the log book, passing on guest requests quickly, helping each other at busy times, and treating each other with respect.
markingPoints: Names at least four villa jobs
Describes the duties of each correctly
Explains the villa manager's role in planning and standards
Shares information through briefings and the log book; passes on requests quickly
Helps each other at busy times and works with respect

essays.stem: Explain how a villa worker can plan their career and develop their skills in the hospitality industry.
essays.modelAnswer: First, the worker should think about where they want to be in a few years, for example moving from housekeeper to housekeeping supervisor, from kitchen assistant to cook, or later to villa manager. They should find out what skills, experience and certificates that job needs, by reading job descriptions and talking to their supervisor. Then they can make a simple plan with steps and dates. To develop their skills, they can complete NVQ-J units and short courses through HEART/NSTA Trust, take TPDCo's Team Jamaica training, and learn a foreign language. At work they can ask to learn new tasks, watch skilled colleagues, and take on extra responsibility. They should keep a record of their training and achievements. Reading industry news keeps their knowledge current. Good attendance, a positive attitude and good references from employers also help them move up.
markingPoints: Sets a clear career goal
Finds out what the job needs (job descriptions, talking to the supervisor)
Makes a plan with steps and dates
Takes training: NVQ-J units, HEART/NSTA courses, Team Jamaica, a language
Learns on the job, keeps records, and shows good attendance and attitude

essays.stem: Explain how the tourist seasons and the hurricane season affect villa work in Jamaica.
essays.modelAnswer: The peak or high season runs from about mid-December to mid-April, when winter in North America and Europe sends many visitors to Jamaica. Villas are often fully booked, rates are higher, and staff work long hours with many arrivals and departures, so good planning, stock control and teamwork matter. Some villas take on extra staff. The low season, roughly from late spring to the autumn, is quieter. Villas may offer lower rates and special offers, and staff may have fewer hours. It is a good time for deep cleaning, repairs, painting and training. The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June to November. Villas need a hurricane plan: staff must know how to secure furniture, shutters and the pool area, store water, food and fuel, keep torches and first-aid kits ready, and keep guests informed and safe, following official weather warnings and the manager's instructions.
markingPoints: Peak season about mid-December to mid-April, and why (winter abroad)
Peak season effects: full bookings, long hours, planning and teamwork
Low season: quieter, offers, used for deep cleaning, repairs and training
Hurricane season runs from June to November
Hurricane plan: secure the property, store supplies, follow official warnings, keep guests safe

essays.stem: Describe two current trends in tourism and explain how villa staff can respond to them.
essays.modelAnswer: One trend is that many guests now find, book and judge villas online. They read reviews and look at photos before they book, and they post their own reviews and pictures afterwards. Villa staff can respond by giving excellent service every day, keeping the villa exactly as it looks in the photos, answering messages quickly and politely, and passing problems to the manager quickly so they are fixed before the guest leaves. A second trend is that more visitors want sustainable and authentic experiences. They care about the environment and want to enjoy real Jamaican food, culture and communities. Staff can respond by saving water and energy, cutting waste and plastic, and explaining the villa's green practices to guests. They can serve local dishes and fruit, buy from local farmers, and recommend licensed community tours, local craft and cultural events. Staff should also keep learning, so they can give guests up-to-date advice.
markingPoints: Names a real current trend (for example online booking and reviews)
Explains a sensible staff response to that trend
Names a second real trend (for example sustainable or authentic tourism)
Explains a sensible staff response to the second trend
Shows the need to keep learning to give up-to-date advice

practical1.title: Produce a visitor information guide for a Jamaican resort area
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group one resort area (for example Montego Bay, Ocho Rios, Negril, Port Antonio or the south coast). Using reliable sources (maps, brochures, the JTB and TPDCo websites, and the Centre's books), produce a large poster or a two-page leaflet that a villa could give to its guests. It must cover: where the area is and how to get there from the nearest international airport; the kinds of places to stay; at least four attractions or activities; local food to try; visitor safety tips; emergency numbers (police 119; fire and ambulance 110); and a list of the sources you used, with their dates. Each member researches and writes at least one section, and the group checks the facts together. Then each member presents their section to the assessor. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group, with the finished guide.
materials: A map of Jamaica and of the resort area
Brochures, books or printed pages about the area
A computer, tablet or phone with internet access, if the Centre allows
Poster paper or A4 paper, markers, glue and scissors
A sources sheet for recording each source and its date
photos: The group's plan, showing each member's section
A screen or page from a reliable source being used for research
The draft sections being checked by the group
checklist: Researched their section using reliable, up-to-date sources
Wrote their section clearly, in plain words
Facts about the location, airport and attractions are correct
Included visitor safety tips and the right emergency numbers
Presented their section clearly and answered a question
Worked well with the group and checked others' facts respectfully
safety: Use scissors carefully and keep them closed when not in use
Use only websites the Centre allows, and do not share personal details online
Keep cables and bags out of walkways

practical2.title: Prepare job cards and a career map for villa services, with an industry news board
practical2.brief: Your group is making a display for new trainees about careers in villa services. Each member chooses a different villa job (for example villa manager, butler, cook, housekeeper, gardener or pool attendant, or driver) and makes a job card showing the main duties, the skills and qualities needed, the training or certificates that help (such as NVQ-J units and Team Jamaica), and the next job up the career ladder. Each member also interviews another member, the assessor or a guest speaker for two minutes about their own work or career, and notes the answers. Then the group puts the job cards on a career map showing how a worker could move up, and adds an industry news board with three recent news items about Jamaican tourism, each with its source and date. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group, with the job cards, the interview notes and the display.
materials: Card or A4 paper, poster paper, markers, glue and pins
Sample job descriptions, or a list of villa jobs from the assessor
A computer, tablet or phone with internet access if the Centre allows, or recent newspapers
A display board or wall space
photos: A member carrying out the two-minute interview
A research screen or newspaper page used for a news item
The career map with the job cards in place
The industry news board with sources and dates
checklist: Completed a job card with correct duties, skills, training and the next career step
Carried out an interview and wrote clear notes
Found at least one recent news item from a reliable source, with its date
Helped arrange the career map in a sensible order
Explained their job card clearly to the assessor
Worked politely and shared tasks fairly
safety: Use pins and scissors with care and put them away after use
Use only websites the Centre allows
Keep walkways clear while building the display
Ask permission before photographing anyone during the interviews
